dialogue.agent: Hello, how may I help you today?

dialogue.user: Hi there! I'm looking for a new book, and I have a few specific things in mind. I'm hoping to find something that's both educational and humorous, with a really high customer rating. My budget for this is between $60 and $150. Could you tell me what you have that fits those criteria?
dialogue.agent: It looks like we don't have any books that match all of your criteria right now. Would you like to broaden your search with different keywords or adjust the price range or rating?

dialogue.user:
That's a bit disappointing. I was really hoping to find something.

Let's try adjusting the criteria. For the rating, I'm looking for at least 5/5.0. What if we relax the *humor* aspect for now and focus on books that are *advice* or *educational*, still within my $60-$150 budget and with that 5/5.0 rating? How does that look?
dialogue.agent:
I found one book that meets your criteria:

**A Little Glide** - This book is priced at $64.99 and has a perfect 5/5.0 rating. It has 2 reviews. The description indicates it contains poems with wit, wisdom, and humane observations, with some pieces appearing in The Nation and The New York Times.

products.title: A Little Glide
products.description: Review As exciting as the life is in these poems, as much history and society and nature as we are given, as much family, as much Americana, the real activity here is the activity of making language physical, of making it as palpable and concrete as what it represents. --Vijay Seshadri, Winner of the 2014 Pulitzer Prize for 3 Sections (Graywolf Press, 2013)These poems skewer and empathize in equal parts. I love them because they are witty, prickly, friendly and wise, formally rigorous and improvisatory, complicated, literary and down to earth, unsparing and most of all terrifically humane. --Daisy Fried, Finalist for the 2007 National Book Critics Circle Award, and author of Women s Poetry: Poems and Advice (Pitt Poetry Series, 2013)Glide of the dance. Of the bird in flight (a raptor, perhaps?). Glide of a plane to another continent, of a life from role to role, stage to stage....O, brave poet! Who finds so much beauty, never flinching from the cruelties of nature all around and the nature that is trapped in us. --Elaine Terranova, Winner of the Walt Whitman Award, and author of Dames Rocket (Penstroke Press, 2012) and Dollhouse (Off the Grid Press, 2013) About the Author Joan Hutton Landis is the author of "That Blue Repair" (Penstroke Press, 2008). Her poems have been set to music by the composer Chris Rogerson and performed at Carnegie Hall. Poems in this book have appeared, or are forthcoming in "The Nation," "The New York Times," "Poetry," "Salmagundi," and in the anthology "Liberation: New Works on Freedom from Internationally Renowned Poets." A graduate of Bennington College, Wesleyan, and Bryn Mawr, Joan lived as a young woman in France, Saudi Arabia, and Lebanon, and subsequently taught literature and poetry workshops for many years at the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia, where she was Chair of the Liberal Arts Department.

Hmm, "A Little Glide" at $64.99 with a 5/5.0 rating sounds promising in terms of quality and price. The description mentions "wit" and "humane observations," which could lean towards the educational and even humorous aspects I'm looking for. However, you mentioned it only has 2 reviews. While the rating is perfect, I generally prefer to see a larger number of reviews to feel more confident about the overall customer satisfaction, especially with a price point in my preferred range.

Could you tell me a bit more about the *content* of the poems? Are they more philosophical, practical advice, or observational humor?

The description for **A Little Glide** mentions that the poems "skewer and empathize in equal parts" and are "witty, prickly, friendly and wise, formally rigorous and improvisatory, complicated, literary and down to earth, unsparing and most of all terrifically humane."

The reviews suggest the content is quite varied, touching upon personal past experiences, observations of life, nature, family, and even philosophical reflections. One reviewer describes it as a "compressed memoir in verse" and another notes the poems range from "bedroom, bathroom, and Joyce's 'noise in the street'" to more profound themes. It seems to be a rich, observational, and reflective collection rather than a source of practical advice.

top_reviews.title: I highly recommend, do not miss this book!
top_reviews.text: The reach of this beautiful book is breathtaking. From a story of a single shoe abandoned by the side of the road, to a fight among girls at school,  to a visit to grandchildren, to love, passion, life and death, everything is in these few pages. This book is about humanity.  Detail illuminates every scene inescapably, insights are so penetrating, and some topics are so risky that they must be viewed as a reflection in Perseus' shield.  It's a global journey from Morristown to Paris to Lebanon,  it includes life and the afterlife, a prodigy of classics by an author of towering personal culture, who holds the entire world in her heart.  Bravo!

top_reviews.title: And then the wonderful culminating poem
top_reviews.text:
JONATHAN FRANZEN, the great novelist
wrote this this note me after reading my book of poems on January 16, 2017.

"But what a book! The trenchancy, the fire, the boldness of linguistic play. I was most taken with the poems that (seem to! presumably!) draw on your personal past; so taken, that the book seemed to me something of an intensely compressed memoir in verse; as if you'd allowed me access to a passionate secret, Joan, I'd hitherto had to only guess was there. And then the wonderful culminating poem, "Autobiography," which I read aloud three times to Kathy. All in all, I was even more moved than impressed, and I was plenty impressed."

This is from PHIL WEINSTEIN, professor emeritus of English literature at Swarthmore College. Oct. 5, 2016

I've now read them all--at quite different times and places, at home on the Vineyard, in the air while flying, and (just now) in our rented Paris flat. I want to try to convey to you some of my pleasure in reading you.

First, the verve, the delight in getting words to cuddle with each other or slap each other down (all those cavorting internal rhymes). I have an abiding sense of the war against your body's defections that you're waging with your words' jaunty capacity--for combat, drama, motive, the look and feel of things. The one is pulling you down--you fear you'll end in a puddle of drool--but how the other lifts you up. You fly high in these poems.

Not that they're reaching for the sublime (even the ones that do seem to do so self-mockingly). Your volume sits solidly on the earth: it is at ease with bedroom, bathroom, and Joyce's "noise in the street."

But most of all, as you say in one of the poems (can't find the line now), you've reached an age where anything may remind you provocatively of something else. Proust speaks of the embroidered texture of memory that arrives when every vignette seems to summon other vignettes: an embarras de richesse playing against the poverty of one's nonverbal now. No sense here of protocols or constraints that would keep certain experiences off-limits. The memories that you turn into poems need carry no special significance to get your attention, no supplementary capacity to symbolize/mean something else and more. (They do mean more, but they seem to qualify--to start off--as just themselves.)

These are also of course the poems of a lifetime lover of poetry.... How these poems suckle at the literary tit! They are fed by the literature you've absorbed, and now casually recycle in a language that is all your own, yet steeped in the phrasing of others.

I want to close on the note of joy. I have a sense of how much pain lies mutely beneath the poems, but the key term is mutely. What you've written sings with a delight in revisiting experience and working it into form. You seem to have reached a point where there's nothing you might not want to try to say. For me at least, your repeated acts of saying communicate joy, and for this I am grateful.

Phil

While "A Little Glide" certainly sounds like it has literary merit and depth, the reviews and description don't strongly suggest it's *educational* in a practical sense, nor overtly *humorous* beyond what might be considered witty observations. It seems more like a collection of personal reflections and observations.

Given that, and still prioritizing that 5/5.0 rating and my budget, do you have any other books that might lean more towards giving *advice* or being genuinely *educational*, perhaps with a bit more substance in terms of reviews?
